This is a longitudinal study with intervention and comparison areas, not a randomised controlled trial. While TBAs are involved (>85% of deliveries), the study design does not meet the RCT requirement.
This is a community-based observational study comparing outcomes of infants delivered at TMHs vs hospitals/home. It is not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a policy document/review about the Safe Motherhood Initiative, not a primary research study or RCT.
The abstract describes a study about Episcopal priests and identity work, completely unrelated to TBAs or maternal health. This appears to be a mismatched abstract.

While this is a community randomized trial, the intervention focuses on training health and nutrition workers for feeding practices. TBAs are only one of many counselling channels (32% at birth), not the primary focus. The study does not compare trained vs untrained TBAs.
This is a methodological paper about meta-analysis techniques, not a primary study about TBAs or maternal health.

This is a cluster-randomized controlled trial involving 62,366 infants across six countries. It compares birth attendants trained in Essential Newborn Care and Neonatal Resuscitation Program versus control clusters without training. This directly meets the criteria of comparing trained versus untrained TBAs.
This is a prospective study examining women's recall accuracy of obstetric complications. It is not a randomised controlled trial and does not involve TBA training comparisons.
This is a cross-sectional survey of 93 TBAs examining their knowledge, attitudes, and practices. While it mentions trained vs untrained TBAs, it is not a randomised controlled trial.

This study compares intervention vs non-intervention areas where TBAs were trained to use misoprostol. However, the abstract does not indicate randomisation - it appears to be a quasi-experimental design rather than an RCT.
This is a review/overview article about neonatal mortality epidemiology, not a primary research study or RCT.

This is a cluster-randomised trial comparing intervention clusters (where LHWs work with TBAs to deliver maternal/newborn care) versus control clusters receiving routine care. The intervention involves TBAs as part of the community-based strategy, meeting the criteria of comparing women cared for in areas served by TBAs with intervention versus routine care.
This is a validation study of verbal autopsy methodology for neonatal deaths. It is not a randomised controlled trial and does not involve TBA training comparisons.
